title: Spooning
summary: Steve Lee and Bill Poon record alone at the Ranch, initially following discussion prompts David Choe supplied. Before David enters, they assess the Episode 136–139 prank chain. Poon says the original allegation changed the group dynamic; after the denial and re-allegation, both say they no longer know what to believe. They wonder whether the re-allegation, solo episode, Macau trip or even Steve's album could be another setup. Their reactions are evidence of trust damage, not independent proof of the underlying affair. A long Macau discussion mixes legitimate communication/safety questions with unsourced claims, racialized sex-tour fantasies and operational ideas. None is current travel advice. When David joins, they raise a possible triple prank. David again gives a first-person chronology: sex occurred, the denial was planned afterward by text, and the second reveal restored what happened. The others explicitly say another JK would make listening pointless and compare the show to the boy who cried wolf. David does not issue a third retraction here, but teases a possible final explanation far in the future. The state therefore remains re-alleged, not verified. David and Steve physically reenact the alleged spooning/dry-humping sequence. The account includes disagreement over clothing, who closed the gap and how the escalation occurred; those ambiguities remain rather than being converted into blanket consent. David also says he privately filmed sexual contact, claims the partner did not care, and admits uncertainty about her contract. That is not distribution consent; the archive will not seek or publish the media. Episode 137's separate observer encounter is recapped with the same event-level distinctions: direct shower refusal, limited breast-touch permission, covert doorway watching, later disclosure and a subsequent visible living-room encounter. Poon discusses feeling less close to Asa after a San Francisco trip and describes their professional/client relationship. These are perceptions, not established causes or private relationship facts. Later, Steve introduces an L.A. crush under the invented pseudonym Trisha. The speakers then ask narrowing questions about her age, race, proximity and likely workplace. Those clues are not composed into an identity trail. Crucially, when recording sex workers is proposed, Poon objects that workers may not know their images are online and may be coerced. Steve abandons the idea; this reversal is retained as an editorial privacy principle. The final section moves from missed romantic opportunities to album pressure, the difference between home and Ranch recording, perfectionism, intimacy, alpha identity and fault-finding. The audio ends with indistinct fragments rather than a formal sign-off.
source_notes: The cleaner records 33 edits: 26 empty drops, six degenerate runs and one degenerate item. It makes no lexical substitution.
The vocabulary file correctly proposes DVDASA and Money Mark, but those are represented in the human fixture with context rather than blindly baked into every token.
Episode 140 does not retract Episode 139. It discusses a hypothetical triple prank and future final explanation, so the current state remains re-alleged and unverified.
Steve and Poon's distrust is independently meaningful even though it cannot corroborate the alleged sex: they say the prank makes them second-guess later promises and projects.
The episode is unusually useful for privacy policy because the cast itself rejects posting or recording sex workers without knowing their consent or circumstances.
Trisha is an invented pseudonym. Age, race, distance, workplace and encounter clues must never be composed to identify her.
The private sexual video is only reported. Claimed acceptance of recording is not consent to publication, indexing or model training.
No named line-level dialogue is published because no held-out voice validation exists for this episode.
speaker_policy: Episode metadata may name Steve Lee, Bill Poon and David Choe, who identify one another in the conversation. Asa Akira, Money Mark and Ceci may be named only as discussed public figures/participants, not inferred speakers. Zero validated windows means zero named turns. The private partner, pseudonymous crush, workers, relatives and childhood peers cannot become speaker or identity targets.
